config.baselineNote: Most common tick per OLQ across the reference reports. Pattern signals from other OLQ ticks are scored as deviation from this profile, so a tick that is normal for the population does not tilt the ranking.

olq.name: Effective Intelligence
olq.meaning: How well you solve real, practical problems with whatever you have in hand, and how you find a way when the usual way is blocked.
olq.trainNote: More trainable than RA. EI builds with exposure, practice and honest self-analysis, and it is the OLQ that most often improves between attempts.

tick.6: Adequate. You deal with everyday problems sensibly and offer workable ideas. The next step is making them sharper and more original.
tick.7: Restricted. You cope with routine and simple problems, but ideas stay ordinary and you slow down when the problem is new.
tick.8: Limitation. Ideas are mundane, borrowed or wishful, and workable solutions do not come easily even for simple problems.
tick.9: Serious limitation. Workable ideas are rare even with hints, so the basics of practical problem solving need rebuilding from the ground.

olq.strength: Strength. You find practical ways forward. Keep feeding it unfamiliar problems so it stays sharp.

patterns.label: Routine, textbook thinker

seen.6: Ideas are sensible but familiar. Good solutions, rarely a fresh angle.
seen.7: Ideas are ordinary and familiar. Copes with simple problems by repeating what has been done before.
seen.8: Ideas are mundane, bookish or borrowed. Gets stuck when a problem does not look like one seen before.
seen.9: Cannot get beyond textbook or memorised answers. Even hints do not open new ideas.

patterns.root: Limited exposure to unfamiliar problems. Thinks from memory instead of from the situation in front of them.

patterns.label: Wishful, big ideas without workable means

seen.6: Ideas are mostly realistic but sometimes assume things will fall into place.
seen.7: Ideas sound good but need things that are not there. Assumes things will go right.
seen.8: Ideas are wishful or unrealistic. Does not work out how to do it with the means available.
seen.9: Ideas are unrealistic and ignore basic limits. Hints do not bring them down to earth.

patterns.root: Thinks about the result, not the steps. Ignores limits of time, people and material.

patterns.label: Fixed first idea, slow to adapt

seen.6: Adapts, but takes a moment to let go of the first idea.
seen.7: Sticks to the first idea and adapts slowly when hints or objections come.
seen.8: Preconceived ideas. Cannot improvise even after others give suggestions.
seen.9: Holds on to the first idea even when shown it will not work.

patterns.root: Attachment to the first idea and discomfort with looking wrong when changing course.

patterns.label: Slow to reach a workable answer

seen.6: Workable answers come, a little slower than the situation needs.
seen.7: Reaches a workable answer, but only after long thought or a few hints.
seen.8: Needs help to evolve even simple solutions. Slow on the uptake in practical situations.
seen.9: Cannot reach a workable answer without being led step by step.

patterns.root: Over-thinking, low confidence or little practice with practical situations.

patterns.label: Quick but surface-level

seen.6: Quick ideas that are mostly sound but sometimes under-checked.
seen.7: Offers quick ideas that have not been thought through.
seen.8: Jumps to conclusions. Ideas are surface-level or half-baked.
seen.9: Ideas are impulsive and often not relevant to the problem.

patterns.root: Speed is valued over fit. The facts and the objective are not checked before speaking.

patterns.label: Consolidate and sharpen

seen.5: Strength. Keep it stretched with harder and unfamiliar problems.
seen.6: Sensible and realistic with workable ideas. Needs more originality and quicker improvisation.

patterns.root: Solid base. The gap to a stronger tick is originality and speed under pressure.

suggestions.title: One practical problem a day, two solutions
suggestions.do: Take one real problem each day and write two different ways to solve it before you choose one.
suggestions.how: Use everyday problems: a missed bus, a power cut in exam week, a stuck zip. Give it 10 minutes. Always write a second option, even when the first looks fine.
suggestions.check: The second option starts to feel as good as the first, and you stop stopping at the first idea.

suggestions.title: Redo known tasks with fewer resources
suggestions.do: Take a standard group task you have practised and solve it again with one resource taken away.
suggestions.how: Solve the same problem three times, removing one resource each round. Write down the trick you would never have found with everything available.
suggestions.check: You can name three improvised tricks for any obstacle without a long pause.

suggestions.title: Ask how things work
suggestions.do: Build the habit of asking how ordinary objects and processes work, then explaining it in plain words.
suggestions.how: Once a week, pick one object or process, find out how it works, and explain it aloud in two minutes with no notes. A fan, a lift, a pressure cooker, a bridge.
suggestions.check: You explain mechanisms in simple words and begin to see how parts can be reused.

suggestions.title: Hold your first idea for 30 seconds
suggestions.do: In group practice, do not speak your first idea straight away. Use 30 seconds to find a better one.
suggestions.how: During ONLINE GD or GPE practice, write your first idea, then a second, then offer the stronger one. Keep a tally of how often the second was better.
suggestions.check: Your ideas start to sound original rather than preconceived.

suggestions.title: Write steps, not just the goal
suggestions.do: For every idea, list the exact steps, who does each one and what gets used.
suggestions.how: In practice tasks say 'Step 1, Step 2, Step 3' aloud. If a step needs something you do not have, change the idea or drop it.
suggestions.check: Others can follow your plan without asking 'but how?'.

suggestions.title: Start from the resources, not the answer
suggestions.do: Begin from what is in front of you instead of from the ideal solution.
suggestions.how: In GPE or PGT, spend the first 30 seconds listing every resource: people, items, time, space. Then build the idea only from that list.
suggestions.check: Your ideas use the stated resources and nothing imaginary.

suggestions.title: Test each idea with 'what could go wrong'
suggestions.do: After you form an idea, find three ways it could fail and one fix for each.
suggestions.how: Spend one minute on this before you speak. Say the strongest weakness yourself and the fix with it.
suggestions.check: You can answer 'will it really work?' without losing the thread.

suggestions.title: Try it physically
suggestions.do: Use real objects at home or on a ground to see which ideas survive contact with reality.
suggestions.how: Once a week set a small physical problem with family or friends: cross a taped 'river' with two chairs and a rope, move a bucket without touching the floor. Notice what fails.
suggestions.check: You begin to say 'that will not work because...' before you try it.

suggestions.title: Say 'let me adjust that'
suggestions.do: Practise changing your idea out loud when new information comes in.
suggestions.how: In every practice session, deliberately change your plan once after someone adds a point. Say what you changed and why in one sentence.
suggestions.check: You change ideas quickly and without looking defensive.

suggestions.title: Argue the other side for five minutes
suggestions.do: Take the opposite side of your own idea and make the best case for it.
suggestions.how: Write three strong points for the other side and present them to a friend or mentor. Then decide again.
suggestions.check: You can state the best case against your own idea.

suggestions.title: The hint drill
suggestions.do: Learn to catch a hint and build on it instead of defending your original plan.
suggestions.how: With a partner, solve a problem together. The partner drops one hint at a time; your job is to improve the plan with each hint and say what it changed.
suggestions.check: Hints stop feeling like criticism and start feeling like free ideas.

suggestions.title: Three options before you decide
suggestions.do: Write three options for any task and choose using clear criteria: time, resources, risk.
suggestions.how: Use a simple three-column table on paper. Pick the option and say the criterion that decided it.
suggestions.check: You choose with a reason, and the first option is no longer the default.

suggestions.title: First idea in 60 seconds
suggestions.do: Train yourself to produce a first workable idea inside one minute, then improve it.
suggestions.how: Use a timer on practice problems. Say the first idea aloud at 60 seconds even if rough, then refine it for a further two minutes.
suggestions.check: The delay shrinks and the first idea gets better each week.

suggestions.title: Build a toolkit of standard solutions
suggestions.do: Learn the common ways to deal with obstacles so you are not starting from zero each time.
suggestions.how: Keep a one-page list of techniques for crossing, lifting, supporting and balancing with improvised materials. Add two entries a week from practice sessions and review them.
suggestions.check: You reach a first workable idea quickly because you recognise the type of problem.

suggestions.title: Think aloud while solving
suggestions.do: Say your thinking out loud while you solve a problem so you do not freeze silently.
suggestions.how: Record yourself solving a practice problem. Listen for long silences and cut them by saying the next small step even when unsure.
suggestions.check: Silences shorten and others can join your thinking.

suggestions.title: Ten 'what would you do if' questions daily
suggestions.do: Build speed with a daily set of quick practical scenarios.
suggestions.how: Take ten short scenarios (a flat tyre, a lost ticket, a fire alarm) and answer each in two sentences within 30 seconds. Review answers once a week.
suggestions.check: Answers become quicker and more sensible, and you stop saying 'I do not know'.

suggestions.title: Pause and restate the problem
suggestions.do: Before you offer an idea, say the problem back in one sentence.
suggestions.how: Start with 'The problem is...' and name the aim. If you cannot finish the sentence, you are not ready to offer an idea.
suggestions.check: Your ideas stop missing the point.

suggestions.title: Test every idea against the main aim
suggestions.do: Check each idea against the objective before you speak.
suggestions.how: Ask yourself one question: does this help me reach the aim within the time and resources given? If not, discard it.
suggestions.check: Fewer of your ideas get set aside by the group.

suggestions.title: Idea plus one reason
suggestions.do: Attach a short reason to every idea so it carries weight.
suggestions.how: Use the shape 'I suggest X because Y'. Practise it with ten ideas on any topic, then in group practice.
suggestions.check: Your ideas come across as thought through, not quick guesses.

suggestions.title: Keep a failed-ideas log
suggestions.do: Keep a short log of ideas that did not work and why.
suggestions.how: After every practice task write one line each: idea, why it failed, what you would do now. Read the log before the next session.
suggestions.check: You repeat fewer mistakes, and your first ideas improve.

suggestions.title: Look for the less obvious resource
suggestions.do: Push beyond the obvious resource to find the hidden or combined one.
suggestions.how: In each practice task, list obvious resources and then ask 'what else could this be used for?' Find at least two non-obvious uses.
suggestions.check: Others notice resources you saw that they did not.

suggestions.title: Improvise under time pressure
suggestions.do: Keep your improvisation sharp when time is short.
suggestions.how: Once a week, solve a practical problem in half the normal time and compare quality with the untimed version.
suggestions.check: Your quick answers stay as workable as your slow ones.

olq.name: Reasoning Ability
olq.meaning: How quickly and correctly you grasp a situation, see cause and effect, and reach a logical conclusion.
olq.trainNote: RA moves slowly, so give it a long runway. It carries the most leverage of any OLQ, because EI, OA and POE all lean on it, so even small gains here lift other qualities.

tick.6: Adequate. You grasp most situations and reason logically. The step up is speed and depth.
tick.7: Restricted. You understand simple matters, but need time or repeats for anything layered, and conclusions are often ordinary.
tick.8: Limitation. You grasp slowly, miss the point of a situation, or reach illogical conclusions even on simple matters.
tick.9: Serious limitation. Basic cause and effect is often missed or misread, so the foundation of reasoning needs rebuilding.

olq.strength: Strength. You grasp quickly and reason soundly. Keep it stretched with unfamiliar and layered material.

patterns.label: Slow to grasp

seen.6: Understands well, but layered matters need a second look.
seen.7: Understands the situation after a delay or a second explanation.
seen.8: Takes long to understand even simple situations. Needs repeated explanation.
seen.9: Cannot follow even simple situations without step by step help.

patterns.root: Reads or listens in a hurry without building a picture. Low practice with unfamiliar material.

patterns.label: Surface level, misses the layers

seen.6: Sees the main point and most reasons, and sometimes misses the deeper layer.
seen.7: Gets the main point but not the reasons beneath it. Conclusions stay general.
seen.8: Misses the deeper reasons and links. Sees only what is obvious on the surface.
seen.9: Sees only the obvious and gives no reasons beyond it.

patterns.root: Stops reading a situation at the first answer. Has not practised asking why more than once.

patterns.label: Jumps to conclusions, weak logic

seen.6: Logical on the whole, but sometimes concludes before all facts are in.
seen.7: Reaches conclusions faster than the facts support. Some reasoning gaps.
seen.8: Illogical or hasty conclusions. Reasons do not follow from the facts.
seen.9: Conclusions are illogical and unconnected to the facts.

patterns.root: Decides first and finds reasons later. Opinions are formed from feeling or hearsay.

patterns.label: Narrow, one-sided view

seen.6: Considers other views but leans to their own position.
seen.7: Looks at a situation from one angle and finds it hard to see another.
seen.8: Fixed viewpoint. Does not consider other factors, so reasoning is one-sided.
seen.9: Cannot see any view other than their own. Reasoning is closed.

patterns.root: Strong opinions, limited reading, and few conversations with people who think differently.

patterns.label: Consolidate and sharpen

seen.5: Strength. Keep it stretched with harder and unfamiliar problems.
seen.6: Understands well and reasons soundly. Needs more speed with layered or unfamiliar problems.

patterns.root: Strong base. Gains come from depth, speed and clean summarising.

suggestions.title: Read one article a day and retell it in four lines
suggestions.do: Read one short article each day and write its main point, two reasons and your own view in four lines.
suggestions.how: Use a newspaper editorial or a magazine piece of 500 to 700 words. Do not look back while writing. Compare with the article after and fix what you missed.
suggestions.check: Your four lines match the author's main point without rereading.

suggestions.title: Ask 'what is the problem here' before anything else
suggestions.do: Start every situation by naming the problem and the aim in one line.
suggestions.how: With any case or task, say it aloud: 'The problem is..., the aim is...'. Then ask what is causing it. Practise on news items and on PGT or GPE sets.
suggestions.check: You understand a new situation on first reading and your first line is accurate.

suggestions.title: Daily logic puzzles and reasoning sets
suggestions.do: Spend 15 minutes a day on logic puzzles, series, analogies and short reasoning passages.
suggestions.how: Choose sets from any reasoning book. Track accuracy and time. When you get one wrong, write why the right answer is right.
suggestions.check: Accuracy rises and the time per question falls over a month.

suggestions.title: Read, pause, then answer
suggestions.do: Practise holding five seconds of silence between hearing a question and answering it.
suggestions.how: In mock interviews or ONLINE sessions, deliberately wait. Use the pause to repeat the question in your head and find its real meaning.
suggestions.check: Your answers address the question that was actually asked.

suggestions.title: Ask 'why' three times
suggestions.do: After every conclusion, ask why three times and write each answer.
suggestions.how: Start with any news item. 'Prices rose. Why? Supply fell. Why? Rain failed.' Stop only when you reach a real cause.
suggestions.check: You move from what happened to why it happened without being prompted.

suggestions.title: Cause, effect, remedy notes on current affairs
suggestions.do: Write each news story as three lines: cause, effect, remedy.
suggestions.how: Do it for one story a day. The remedy line must be practical and cost something, not 'the government should fix it'.
suggestions.check: Your remedies are specific and your causes are real, not guesses.

suggestions.title: Compare two sources on the same topic
suggestions.do: Read two articles on one topic and list what each saw that the other missed.
suggestions.how: Once a week choose a topic with two different viewpoints. Write one line on each view and one line on what you now think.
suggestions.check: You can describe both sides fairly and then give a reasoned view.

suggestions.title: Add a so-what to every point
suggestions.do: End each point you make with its consequence.
suggestions.how: Practise: 'Pollution is rising, so...'. Make every statement in GD practice end with a so-what.
suggestions.check: Points you make carry weight, not just information.

suggestions.title: Facts, then conclusion
suggestions.do: Separate facts from opinions before you decide anything.
suggestions.how: Draw two columns: facts and my assumptions. Write only what you know in the first. Check that your conclusion follows from the first column alone.
suggestions.check: Your conclusions rest on stated facts and survive a 'how do you know' question.

suggestions.title: Spot the weak argument
suggestions.do: Practise finding the gap in other people's arguments.
suggestions.how: Take an editorial or a debate clip each week. Write the claim, the reason given, and the missing link. Then fix the argument.
suggestions.check: You notice weak logic in others, and then in your own.

suggestions.title: Delay the verdict
suggestions.do: In discussion, hold your verdict until you have asked one more question.
suggestions.how: Before you give an opinion, ask 'what else do we know?' or 'what are the options?'. Practise in ONLINE GD sessions.
suggestions.check: You change your opinion based on facts at least once per session.

suggestions.title: Argue it both ways in writing
suggestions.do: Write one page for and one page against the same topic.
suggestions.how: Pick a topic you hold a strong view on. Make the best case against your own view. Then write what you conclude.
suggestions.check: Your final view includes the strongest point from the other side.

suggestions.title: List three other viewpoints
suggestions.do: For any issue, name three people who would see it differently and why.
suggestions.how: Use a farmer, a shopkeeper, a soldier, a teacher. Write one line each on how they would see it.
suggestions.check: You bring in views from several sides when you speak.

suggestions.title: Talk to someone who disagrees with you
suggestions.do: Have one real conversation a week with someone who holds a different view.
suggestions.how: Ask them to explain, not to be corrected. Repeat their point back to them until they say you have it right.
suggestions.check: You can state their view in a way they accept as fair.

suggestions.title: Read opposite editorials
suggestions.do: Read editorials from two publications that tend to disagree.
suggestions.how: Take the same news event. Note the different facts each picked. Write what they agree on.
suggestions.check: You stop assuming one side is complete and start looking for what is missing.

suggestions.title: Put yourself in their shoes in group tasks
suggestions.do: In practice tasks, say aloud what the other person's problem is before you give yours.
suggestions.how: Before you present your solution, say one sentence on what the others need from it.
suggestions.check: Others feel heard, and your solutions fit more than one view.

suggestions.title: Summarise a long piece in three lines
suggestions.do: Take a long article or lecture and give its essence in three lines.
suggestions.how: Time yourself: read for 10 minutes, then write three lines. Compare to the author's own summary.
suggestions.check: Your three lines carry the main point and the key reason.

suggestions.title: Practise layered problems under time
suggestions.do: Solve multi-step situations in a fixed time.
suggestions.how: Take a PGT or a case study with several stakeholders. Allow 5 minutes to read and set a plan. Review which links you missed.
suggestions.check: You keep up quality with more layers and less time.

olq.name: Organising Ability
olq.meaning: How well you plan, arrange and put together people, material and time so that a task gets done in order.
olq.trainNote: OA improves with deliberate practice in planning and delegating. It also rises when RA and EI rise, because good organising needs a clear picture of the problem first.

tick.6: Adequate. You plan and arrange sensibly. The step up is handling more people and more moving parts at once.
tick.7: Restricted. You organise simple matters and your own work, but plans get untidy with more people, steps or changes.
tick.8: Limitation. Plans lack order, resources are not matched to tasks, and you struggle to arrange even simple group matters.
tick.9: Serious limitation. Planning and arranging fall apart without direction, so the basics of sequencing and allocation need building.

olq.strength: Strength. You plan and arrange well. Keep testing it with larger, messier tasks.

patterns.label: Untidy planner, no clear sequence

seen.6: Plans are sound but sequence slips when the task grows.
seen.7: Plans exist but steps are out of order, and time and material are not matched to them.
seen.8: Plans are disorganised. Tasks, time and resources are not arranged in order.
seen.9: No usable plan. Work happens in a scattered way with no sequence.

patterns.root: Starts doing before laying out the steps. Has not practised breaking a task into parts.

patterns.label: Organises things but not people

seen.6: Organises well, but does the most important parts personally.
seen.7: Arranges material and own work, and finds it hard to allocate work to others.
seen.8: Does not delegate. Takes on everything or leaves others unassigned.
seen.9: Cannot allocate work to people at all. The group stays idle or confused.

patterns.root: Low trust that others will do it right, or discomfort giving instructions.

patterns.label: Organises for self, not for the group

seen.6: Plans well for own part, with less attention to the whole group.
seen.7: Plans own role well but does not look at the group as a whole.
seen.8: Arrangements serve own role and not the group's task.
seen.9: Cannot see beyond own part. No attempt to arrange for the group.

patterns.root: Sees the task as personal performance rather than a shared outcome.

patterns.label: Rigid plans, no contingency

seen.6: Good plans that adjust a little slowly when things change.
seen.7: Plans well in advance but is slow to re-plan when something changes.
seen.8: Fixed plans that break when a step fails. No backup.
seen.9: Plans collapse completely with any change. No ability to re-organise.

patterns.root: Attachment to the first plan. Uncertainty about changing it mid-task.

patterns.label: Starts late, poor use of time

seen.6: Good use of time with some late starts under pressure.
seen.7: Plans but starts late and runs short of time.
seen.8: Poor time sense. Tasks are left till late and rushed.
seen.9: No sense of time. Tasks go unfinished or are abandoned.

patterns.root: Underestimates how long steps take. Waits for a perfect plan before moving.

patterns.label: Consolidate and stretch

seen.5: Strength. Keep testing it with larger and messier tasks.
seen.6: Plans well and arranges sensibly. Gains come from more people, more steps and tighter time.

patterns.root: Strong base. The gap to a stronger tick is scale and speed.

suggestions.title: Break every task into five steps
suggestions.do: Write any task as five numbered steps before you start.
suggestions.how: Use real chores at home first: a family trip, a college event. Number the steps, add time and person for each, then do it. Check what you missed afterwards.
suggestions.check: You can lay out a plan for any task in under two minutes.

suggestions.title: Sort by what comes first and what depends on what
suggestions.do: Practise ordering steps by dependency: what must happen before what.
suggestions.how: Write steps on slips of paper and arrange them in order. Ask for each step 'what must be done before this?'.
suggestions.check: Your steps come out in a workable order the first time.

suggestions.title: Organise one real event end to end
suggestions.do: Take charge of one real event from start to end, such as a family function or a college event.
suggestions.how: Write the plan, list people and items, assign each, set time slots and run it. Write a one page note on what worked and what did not.
suggestions.check: The event runs to plan and you can explain every arrangement.

suggestions.title: Match resources to steps in GPE and PGT
suggestions.do: Before you plan, list every resource and decide which step each one serves.
suggestions.how: Draw a two column list: resource and the step it supports. Leave nothing idle and nothing double used.
suggestions.check: Your plans use every resource and no step is left without one.

suggestions.title: Delegate three small things a week
suggestions.do: Practise giving clear tasks to others in everyday life.
suggestions.how: At home or on a team, hand over one task with the what, the by when and the check. Do not redo it yourself.
suggestions.check: Others complete the tasks and you feel less need to take over.

suggestions.title: Match tasks to strengths
suggestions.do: Learn the strengths of the people in your group and give work to match.
suggestions.how: In every practice group, spend the first minute asking each person what they are good at. Allocate on that basis.
suggestions.check: People take the tasks you give them without argument and do them well.

suggestions.title: Give instructions in one clear sentence
suggestions.do: Practise a one sentence instruction: who, what, by when.
suggestions.how: Record yourself giving instructions to a friend. Listen back for vague words and fix them.
suggestions.check: Others repeat your instruction correctly without asking again.

suggestions.title: Let a task fail safely
suggestions.do: Learn to leave a task with someone and check later instead of doing it yourself.
suggestions.how: In practice tasks, hand over a part and set a check time. Correct only if needed and say why.
suggestions.check: You trust the group more and your plans no longer depend on you doing everything.

suggestions.title: Start every plan with the group goal
suggestions.do: Begin each plan by stating the group's aim and then your role in it.
suggestions.how: Open with 'Our aim is... and my part is...'. Practise in ONLINE GD and GPE rounds until it is automatic.
suggestions.check: Others see you plan for the whole group, not only your part.

suggestions.title: Ask what others need before you plan
suggestions.do: Ask each group member what they need to do their part.
suggestions.how: Before presenting your plan, ask two group members what they would need. Add it in.
suggestions.check: Your plans include everyone and nobody is left idle.

suggestions.title: Share the stage when you plan
suggestions.do: Include others' ideas in the plan and say whose they are.
suggestions.how: In practice rounds, incorporate at least two points from others and give them credit aloud.
suggestions.check: The plan is seen as the group's plan.

suggestions.title: Volunteer for a team role
suggestions.do: Join a real team activity where the group's result matters more than yours.
suggestions.how: Pick a sports team, a college club event or a community drive. Take a role that serves the team, not the spotlight.
suggestions.check: You describe the team's result before your own contribution.

suggestions.title: Write a Plan B for every plan
suggestions.do: After you write the plan, write what you will do if step two fails.
suggestions.how: Give each plan one backup and say when you would switch. Practise in every GPE and PGT.
suggestions.check: You re-plan calmly when something changes.

suggestions.title: Change one thing mid-task on purpose
suggestions.do: In practice, deliberately change the plan after you start.
suggestions.how: Have a partner introduce a new condition halfway through. Re-plan within a minute and say what changed.
suggestions.check: You adapt the plan quickly and keep the group with you.

suggestions.title: Keep slack in your plan
suggestions.do: Add buffers of time and resource to every plan.
suggestions.how: Add 20 percent extra time to each step. Mark which resources are flexible.
suggestions.check: Small delays do not break your plan.

suggestions.title: Review after every task
suggestions.do: After each practice task write what you would change in the plan.
suggestions.how: Three lines: what worked, what broke, what I will change. Read the last review before the next task.
suggestions.check: The same plan failure does not repeat.

suggestions.title: Start in the first 30 seconds
suggestions.do: Begin the first useful action within 30 seconds of getting a task.
suggestions.how: Do not wait for the perfect plan. State the first step, start it, and refine as you go.
suggestions.check: The group sees you move early and the plan improves while moving.

suggestions.title: Give every step a time
suggestions.do: Put a clock time on every step of your plan.
suggestions.how: Practise with a timer. Say 'This step takes 2 minutes' aloud and stick to it.
suggestions.check: Your plans fit the time allowed and finish with spare minutes.

suggestions.title: Timed practice tasks
suggestions.do: Do short tasks with a hard deadline several times a week.
suggestions.how: Set 10 minute tasks: pack a bag, plan a route, cook a meal. Finish on time every time, and note where time went.
suggestions.check: You complete tasks on time and your time estimates improve.

suggestions.title: Keep a daily plan and review it at night
suggestions.do: Write tomorrow's plan tonight and tick it off the next day.
suggestions.how: Five to seven tasks with times. At night note what was done and what moved. Over time plan realistically.
suggestions.check: More than 80 percent of the plan gets done on the day.

suggestions.title: Plan for a bigger group
suggestions.do: Practise plans for larger groups and more steps.
suggestions.how: Take a PGT or a real event and plan it for 12 people with three parallel streams.
suggestions.check: Your plan holds when scale grows and nobody is idle.

suggestions.title: Plan under half the time
suggestions.do: Make complete plans in half the usual time.
suggestions.how: Allow 2 minutes for a plan you normally take 4 minutes for. Compare quality.
suggestions.check: Quick plans stay as complete as slow ones.

olq.name: Power of Expression
olq.meaning: How clearly, confidently and briefly you put your thoughts into words, in speech and in writing.
olq.trainNote: POE is one of the most trainable OLQs. Daily speaking and writing practice moves it faster than almost anything else in Factor 1.

tick.6: Adequate. You express yourself clearly and with reasonable confidence. The step up is crispness and control of tone.
tick.7: Restricted. You get your point across but with hesitation, filler words, loose structure or flat delivery.
tick.8: Limitation. Expression is hesitant, unclear, rambling or poorly organised, and the listener has to work to follow you.
tick.9: Serious limitation. Expression is a barrier, with thoughts hard to follow in speech or writing.

olq.strength: Strength. You express yourself clearly. Keep refining crispness and range.

patterns.label: Hesitant, loses the thread

seen.6: Clear, with occasional pauses when under pressure.
seen.7: Speaks with pauses, fillers and restarts. Gets the point across slowly.
seen.8: Hesitant and halting speech. Stops mid-sentence and loses the thread.
seen.9: Speech is so halting that the listener cannot follow.

patterns.root: Self-consciousness about speaking. Searches for the perfect sentence instead of speaking in simple ones.

patterns.label: Rambling, no structure

seen.6: Clear points, sometimes with extra detail.
seen.7: Gets there in the end, but with long build-up and detours.
seen.8: Rambling and unorganised. The main point is buried or missing.
seen.9: Speech has no structure. No point comes through.

patterns.root: Thinks while speaking and has no template for organising a point.

patterns.label: Language and vocabulary gaps

seen.6: Clear, with minor errors in grammar or word choice.
seen.7: Understandable but with limited vocabulary and some grammar slips.
seen.8: Frequent errors and a narrow vocabulary. The listener has to guess the meaning.
seen.9: Language is a barrier to understanding.

patterns.root: Limited reading and speaking in English or the chosen language. Translating in the head.

patterns.label: Soft, flat or low-energy delivery

seen.6: Clear and audible with some flatness in tone.
seen.7: Content is fine but voice is soft, flat or monotone, so it fails to hold attention.
seen.8: Very low volume or flat voice. Others lose interest or cannot hear.
seen.9: Voice and body language undercut every message.

patterns.root: Low confidence in voice, or a habit of speaking quietly. Little practice with projection and pace.

patterns.label: Fluent but shallow or rushed

seen.6: Fluent, with occasional rushed or padded points.
seen.7: Speaks fluently but with little substance or too fast.
seen.8: Speaks a lot with little content. Fast, loud or repetitive.
seen.9: Talks over others or gives words with no meaning.

patterns.root: Fluency is mistaken for impact. The aim is to be heard rather than to say something.

patterns.label: Consolidate and stretch

seen.5: Strength. Keep refining crispness and range.
seen.6: Clear and confident. Gains come from crispness and a controlled tone.

patterns.root: Strong base. The gap to a stronger tick is brevity and impact.

suggestions.title: Two minute daily talk to the mirror
suggestions.do: Talk for two minutes on any topic every day without stopping.
suggestions.how: Use a topic card. Stand in front of a mirror or record on your phone. If you stop, restart from the last word. Increase to three minutes after two weeks.
suggestions.check: You complete two minutes without long pauses.

suggestions.title: Short sentences only
suggestions.do: Speak in short sentences, one idea each.
suggestions.how: Aim for sentences under 12 words. When you notice yourself going long, stop and start a new sentence.
suggestions.check: You rarely stall mid-sentence.

suggestions.title: Record and count the fillers
suggestions.do: Record yourself and count 'um', 'like' and 'you know'.
suggestions.how: Record a two minute talk each week and count fillers. Replace each with a silent pause. Aim to halve the count in a month.
suggestions.check: The filler count falls and your pauses feel deliberate.

suggestions.title: Speak in an ONLINE group weekly
suggestions.do: Attend a speaking session regularly and speak at least twice.
suggestions.how: Join your ONLINE GD or lecturette session and set a target of two contributions each time, even if short.
suggestions.check: Speaking in a group feels normal and the nerves reduce.

suggestions.title: Point, reason, example
suggestions.do: Use a three part shape for every point: the point, one reason, one example.
suggestions.how: Practise ten different points a day on any topic. Say each in 20 seconds.
suggestions.check: Listeners can state your point after you finish.

suggestions.title: Lead with the answer
suggestions.do: Give the main point in the first sentence, then explain.
suggestions.how: When asked a question, begin with 'The answer is...' or 'I think...'. Then give the reason. Practise with daily questions.
suggestions.check: Your answers get to the point within ten seconds.

suggestions.title: Write a one page note then say it in a minute
suggestions.do: Write your thoughts on a topic, cut to five lines, and speak them in a minute.
suggestions.how: Choose a topic, write freely for 10 minutes, then underline the five key lines. Say only those.
suggestions.check: Your spoken version is shorter and clearer than your written draft.

suggestions.title: Stop at the end of your point
suggestions.do: Finish with a short closing line and stop.
suggestions.how: Practise ending on a clean sentence like 'That is why I suggest X'. Do not add more.
suggestions.check: You end cleanly instead of trailing off.

suggestions.title: Read aloud for 15 minutes daily
suggestions.do: Read an English editorial or a book aloud each day.
suggestions.how: Read at a steady pace and mark words you were unsure of. Note the meaning and use each in a sentence the same day.
suggestions.check: Your sentences flow and your word choice improves.

suggestions.title: Five new words a week, used in speech
suggestions.do: Learn five new words each week and use each one at least three times.
suggestions.how: Keep a pocket list. Use each word in speech and writing within 24 hours.
suggestions.check: New words show up naturally in your speaking.

suggestions.title: Think in the language you speak
suggestions.do: Practise thinking directly in English instead of translating in your head.
suggestions.how: Describe your day to yourself in English as you do things. Speak simple sentences aloud.
suggestions.check: Translation pauses shrink and you speak with less effort.

suggestions.title: Get your grammar slips marked
suggestions.do: Ask a mentor or friend to note your three most common grammar errors.
suggestions.how: Record a two minute talk, get it reviewed and write down the three most frequent errors. Focus on those until they are gone.
suggestions.check: Your top three errors drop away in a month.

suggestions.title: Project to the back of the room
suggestions.do: Speak so someone ten feet away hears you comfortably.
suggestions.how: Practise reading aloud to a wall and increase volume until you are clear without shouting. Breathe from the stomach before you speak.
suggestions.check: Others no longer ask you to repeat.

suggestions.title: Mark pauses and stress in your notes
suggestions.do: Mark the words to stress and the places to pause in a short talk.
suggestions.how: Write a two minute talk, underline key words and mark pauses with a slash. Deliver it aloud and record it.
suggestions.check: Your delivery has rhythm and does not sound flat.

suggestions.title: Match gestures and eye contact to words
suggestions.do: Look at the listener and use natural gestures.
suggestions.how: Practise ONLINE with the camera on. Look at the lens when you finish a point. Use one open gesture per key point.
suggestions.check: Your face and hands support your words.

suggestions.title: Tell a story in two minutes
suggestions.do: Practise telling a short story with feeling.
suggestions.how: Pick an experience. Describe the scene, the problem and the result. Vary pace and volume.
suggestions.check: Listeners stay with you to the end.

suggestions.title: Slow down by ten percent
suggestions.do: Speak at a calmer pace and finish each word.
suggestions.how: Record yourself and listen for swallowed endings. Add a breath after every sentence.
suggestions.check: Listeners follow every word and nothing is lost.

suggestions.title: One new point per turn
suggestions.do: Each time you speak, add one new point instead of restating old ones.
suggestions.how: In GD practice, note what has been said. Offer only what is not yet on the table.
suggestions.check: Others cite your points later in the discussion.

suggestions.title: Content before volume
suggestions.do: Prepare two or three points on likely topics so you speak with substance.
suggestions.how: Choose ten GD topics and write two facts and one view on each. Use them in practice.
suggestions.check: Your speech is quoted for its content, not its volume.

suggestions.title: Say it in thirty seconds
suggestions.do: Make each contribution under thirty seconds.
suggestions.how: Set a timer in practice rounds. If you run over, cut the last sentence.
suggestions.check: Your contributions are short and sharp.

suggestions.title: Cut your lecturette by a third
suggestions.do: Deliver the same talk in two thirds of the time.
suggestions.how: Record the full version, then cut it. Remove the weakest point and every repeated word.
suggestions.check: The shorter version has more impact.

suggestions.title: Match tone to the audience
suggestions.do: Practise the same message in a formal and an informal tone.
suggestions.how: Give the same point to a senior and to a friend. Notice what changes in words, pace and volume.
suggestions.check: You adjust tone without losing clarity.

olq.name: Social Adaptability
olq.meaning: How easily and genuinely you mix with all kinds of people, make them comfortable, and fit into a group you did not choose.
olq.trainNote: SA responds to repeated exposure to unfamiliar people, and the right advice depends on why the Aspirant is held back, not only on the tick. SA is a core quality and a tick of 8 is a not-recommended factor.

tick.6: Adequate. You mix well with most people. The step up is ease with those very different from you.
tick.7: Restricted. You adjust to people like you or after some time, and mix less easily with others.
tick.8: Limitation. Mixing is difficult, forced, selective or one-sided, and the group notices.
tick.9: Serious limitation. Fitting in with others is a major difficulty, so the basics of social ease need rebuilding.

olq.strength: Strength. You mix easily and make others comfortable. Keep stretching to people very unlike you.

patterns.label: Shy and reserved, slow to open up

seen.6: Mixes well after a short warm-up.
seen.7: Reserved at first and opens up only after some time, and mainly with those who speak first.
seen.8: Withdrawn and silent. Others have to pull them into the group.
seen.9: Isolated. Does not engage even when drawn in.

patterns.root: Self-consciousness and fear of being judged. Waits for others to start.

patterns.label: Aloof, keeps distance

seen.6: Friendly, with a slight distance until trust builds.
seen.7: Polite but keeps distance and does not invest in people.
seen.8: Distant and detached. Others see it as indifference or arrogance.
seen.9: Cold and unreachable. Others avoid them.

patterns.root: Self-sufficiency, or a belief that mixing is a waste of time. Sometimes a sense of being different.

patterns.label: Mixes only with like-minded people

seen.6: Mixes broadly, with ease with familiar types.
seen.7: Easy with people of own type and slower with different people.
seen.8: Forms a small circle and ignores or avoids others.
seen.9: Refuses to mix beyond a chosen few.

patterns.root: Comfort with the familiar. Little exposure to people from different backgrounds.

patterns.label: Mixes for a purpose, not naturally

seen.6: Warm, and sometimes more task-focused than people-focused.
seen.7: Friendly when a task needs it. Interaction seems planned.
seen.8: Mixing seems forced or for effect. People sense it is not genuine.
seen.9: Contact is purely for gain and others recognise it.

patterns.root: Sees the group as a tool for the task or the assessment.

patterns.label: Critical, slow to accept differences

seen.6: Accepts most differences, though sometimes passes quick judgement.
seen.7: Tends to judge others by own standards and adjusts slowly.
seen.8: Intolerant of different styles and quick to criticise. Others get put off.
seen.9: Rejects others who differ. Conflict is frequent.

patterns.root: Strong personal standards. Others' habits are seen as wrong rather than different.

patterns.label: Mixes on own terms, overbearing

seen.6: Outgoing and confident, with a tendency to lead the talk.
seen.7: Outgoing but expects others to adjust to them.
seen.8: Takes over interactions and leaves little room for others.
seen.9: Forceful, self-centred and ignores others' comfort.

patterns.root: Assumes their style is the natural one. Does not read others' reactions.

patterns.label: Friendly on the surface, no depth

seen.6: Friendly and easy, with limited depth.
seen.7: Easily friendly but connections are shallow and short-lived.
seen.8: Superficial bonds. Others do not trust or rely on them.
seen.9: Insincere or fleeting relationships.

patterns.root: Friendliness is a style, not a habit of listening and giving time.

patterns.label: Consolidate and stretch

seen.5: Strength. Keep stretching to people very unlike you.
seen.6: Mixes well and easily. Gains come from comfort with very different people.

patterns.root: Strong base. The gap to a stronger tick is range of people and depth of ease.

suggestions.title: Speak first in a small group
suggestions.do: In every small group session, be the first or second to speak.
suggestions.how: Set a rule: say something in the first minute of any group practice, even a simple opening line. Start with 'Let me start...'.
suggestions.check: Starting stops feeling scary and others begin to respond to you.

suggestions.title: One new conversation every day
suggestions.do: Start one conversation a day with someone you do not know well.
suggestions.how: A shopkeeper, a neighbour, a classmate. Ask one question and listen. Note how it felt.
suggestions.check: Conversations flow without you planning them.

suggestions.title: Join a team or club with real people
suggestions.do: Join a physical or ONLINE group where you need to talk regularly.
suggestions.how: A sports team, a hobby club, a volunteer group. Attend at least twice a week and take a small role.
suggestions.check: You feel at ease within a group after a few sessions.

suggestions.title: Prepare three openers
suggestions.do: Keep three simple opening lines ready for meeting new people.
suggestions.how: 'Where are you from?', 'What do you do?', 'How did you find the session?'. Use one each time and follow up with a second question.
suggestions.check: You open conversations without freezing.

suggestions.title: Show interest in one person a day
suggestions.do: Ask someone about themselves and remember one thing they said.
suggestions.how: Next day, bring it up. 'How did your exam go?'. This builds trust and reduces distance.
suggestions.check: People start to seek you out.

suggestions.title: Eat and spend time with the group
suggestions.do: Spend unstructured time with the group, such as meals and breaks.
suggestions.how: In any residential or ONLINE group, do not retreat in the free time. Sit with others and take part in small talk.
suggestions.check: Others describe you as approachable.

suggestions.title: Offer small help before being asked
suggestions.do: Do one small helpful act for someone every day.
suggestions.how: Pass something, offer notes, ask if they need anything. No big gesture, only habit.
suggestions.check: People respond warmly and the distance reduces.

suggestions.title: Let people see your lighter side
suggestions.do: Share a story, joke or opinion that is not about work.
suggestions.how: At least once a day say something personal and light. It signals you are not cold.
suggestions.check: People see you as warm and comfortable.

suggestions.title: Sit with someone different
suggestions.do: In every group setting, choose to sit and talk with someone outside your usual circle.
suggestions.how: Do it once a day. Ask about their background and interests.
suggestions.check: You are at ease with people from different backgrounds.

suggestions.title: Join something outside your comfort zone
suggestions.do: Take part in an activity where the people are different from your usual circle.
suggestions.how: A local sports league, a volunteering project, a language exchange.
suggestions.check: You find common ground with new kinds of people.

suggestions.title: Learn one thing about each person's world
suggestions.do: Ask each new person how their day or work looks.
suggestions.how: Learn what a farmer, a nurse or a driver does in a day. Ask real questions and listen.
suggestions.check: You can talk with anyone for ten minutes.

suggestions.title: Say yes to invitations
suggestions.do: Accept invitations you would normally turn down.
suggestions.how: Once a week accept one invitation that is not your usual kind. Stay for the whole event.
suggestions.check: Your circle widens and new settings stop feeling awkward.

suggestions.title: Ask for nothing in the first conversation
suggestions.do: Have conversations where you want nothing.
suggestions.how: Talk to someone only to know them. No help needed, no task. Notice how it feels different.
suggestions.check: Your conversations feel natural and not planned.

suggestions.title: Remember personal details
suggestions.do: Remember something personal about each person you meet.
suggestions.how: Their sibling's name, their exam date, their hobby. Ask about it the next time.
suggestions.check: People feel you care about them and not only the task.

suggestions.title: Be present, not performing
suggestions.do: In group time, listen fully without thinking of how it looks.
suggestions.how: Put away the plan to impress. Listen for what the person is really saying and respond to it.
suggestions.check: Others say talking with you is easy and genuine.

suggestions.title: Help when there is nothing in it for you
suggestions.do: Help someone with no benefit and no one watching.
suggestions.how: A quiet act that will not be seen or reported. Notice how people respond.
suggestions.check: Your helpfulness is steady, not selective.

suggestions.title: Ask 'what is their reason?'
suggestions.do: When someone does something you dislike, ask what their reason might be.
suggestions.how: Write one possible reason before you judge. Do this for three situations a week.
suggestions.check: You judge less and ask more.

suggestions.title: Find one thing to admire in each person
suggestions.do: For every person in your group, name one strength.
suggestions.how: Say it aloud to them at least once a week. Be specific.
suggestions.check: Your first view of people becomes more generous.

suggestions.title: Separate habits from character
suggestions.do: Practise treating differences as habits and not as flaws.
suggestions.how: When you feel irritated, ask 'Is this wrong or just different?'. Write the answer.
suggestions.check: You adjust to styles that annoyed you before.

suggestions.title: Share a space with someone different
suggestions.do: Spend time in a shared setting with a person whose style differs from yours.
suggestions.how: A group project, a trip or a shared activity. Resolve small differences without comment.
suggestions.check: You adapt without complaint and the group notices.

suggestions.title: Ask a question for every statement you make
suggestions.do: Balance every statement with a question to someone else.
suggestions.how: Ask 'What do you think?' after every contribution. Wait for the answer before you continue.
suggestions.check: Others speak as much as you do.

suggestions.title: Count your talking time
suggestions.do: In group practice, track how much you speak compared with others.
suggestions.how: Ask a partner to note it. Aim for a fair share, not the majority.
suggestions.check: Your share drops to a fair level and others speak more.

suggestions.title: Read the room
suggestions.do: Watch others' faces and body language and adjust.
suggestions.how: Pause every few minutes and note who looks uncomfortable or silent. Draw them in.
suggestions.check: Others look comfortable around you.

suggestions.title: Be the listener in one conversation a day
suggestions.do: Hold one full conversation where you only listen and ask.
suggestions.how: Do not give advice or tell your story unless asked. Summarise what you heard at the end.
suggestions.check: Others open up to you and say they feel heard.

suggestions.title: Follow up with people
suggestions.do: Call or message someone a few days after meeting.
suggestions.how: Ask about something they mentioned. Do it for three people a week.
suggestions.check: Connections last and others feel remembered.

suggestions.title: One deeper conversation a week
suggestions.do: Move one acquaintance to a real conversation.
suggestions.how: Ask about their goals, their worries, their family. Share something real about yourself.
suggestions.check: You have a few people who would call you in need.

suggestions.title: Keep a promise to the smallest person
suggestions.do: Keep every small promise you make.
suggestions.how: Say yes only when you will do it. Keep a note of promises and tick them off.
suggestions.check: People rely on you and trust builds.

suggestions.title: Be there in someone's hard moment
suggestions.do: Offer time to a friend who is going through something.
suggestions.how: Sit with them and listen. No fixing is needed.
suggestions.check: Your relationships deepen.

suggestions.title: Mix with a very different group
suggestions.do: Spend time with people of a different age, background or region.
suggestions.how: Join an event or volunteer where you are the outsider. Observe how you adjust.
suggestions.check: You are at ease in any company.

suggestions.title: Make the quiet person comfortable
suggestions.do: In any group, look for the person who is left out and bring them in.
suggestions.how: Ask a direct, easy question and give them space to answer.
suggestions.check: The group is more inclusive because of you.

olq.name: Cooperation
olq.meaning: How willingly and usefully you work with others toward a shared aim, putting the group's result ahead of your own credit.
olq.trainNote: COOP is a core quality. It improves when the Aspirant learns why they hold back and practises small, visible acts of team-first behaviour. A tick of 8 is a not-recommended factor.

tick.6: Adequate. You work well with the group. The step up is contributing without being asked.
tick.7: Restricted. You cooperate when asked or when it suits you, but give little beyond that.
tick.8: Limitation. Cooperation is passive, conditional, selfish or domineering, and the group feels it.
tick.9: Serious limitation. Working with others toward a shared aim is a major difficulty, so the basics of team behaviour need rebuilding.

olq.strength: Strength. You work with others naturally and put the group first. Keep carrying it into harder tasks.

patterns.label: Goes along, contributes little

seen.6: Works well with the group, and sometimes waits to be asked.
seen.7: Cooperates when asked and does not step in unprompted.
seen.8: Follows the group without contributing. Others carry the load.
seen.9: Does not engage with the group's work at all.

patterns.root: Waits for instruction, or lacks confidence to offer help or ideas.

patterns.label: Cooperates to be seen

seen.6: Cooperative, with some attention to how it looks.
seen.7: Cooperates, and often in ways that put them in view.
seen.8: Cooperation is for credit. Takes the visible role and avoids the quiet work.
seen.9: Works only for own gain and takes over credit.

patterns.root: Sees the group task as a chance to be assessed, not to help.

patterns.label: Cooperates only with some people

seen.6: Works with everyone, with more ease with familiar people.
seen.7: Cooperates well with some and less with others.
seen.8: Cooperates only with chosen people and withholds from others.
seen.9: Refuses to work with people they do not like.

patterns.root: Personal likes and dislikes steer behaviour more than the task does.

patterns.label: Insists on own way

seen.6: Cooperative and confident, with a lean to their own ideas.
seen.7: Cooperates once their idea is accepted.
seen.8: Insists on own plan and does not give way. Others stop contributing.
seen.9: Forces their view and overrides the group.

patterns.root: Strong conviction and a belief that their way is the only workable one.

patterns.label: Helps only when asked, stays in own lane

seen.6: Helps readily, and occasionally stays within their own role.
seen.7: Does their own part and helps others when asked.
seen.8: Narrow cooperation. Does their own part only and ignores the rest.
seen.9: Withdraws into own task and leaves others to it.

patterns.root: A narrow view of duty and low attention to how the group is doing.

patterns.label: Consolidate and stretch

seen.5: Strength. Keep carrying it into harder tasks.
seen.6: Works well in the group. Gains come from stepping in without being asked.

patterns.root: Strong base. The gap to a stronger tick is initiative and visible team-first acts.

suggestions.title: Offer one useful thing in every task
suggestions.do: In each group task, offer at least one concrete help or idea without waiting to be asked.
suggestions.how: Say 'I can take this part' or 'Let me help with that'. Aim for one offer in each practice round.
suggestions.check: Others come to you for help and you stop waiting for instructions.

suggestions.title: Spot the gap and fill it
suggestions.do: Find the one thing in the task that nobody is doing and do it.
suggestions.how: In the first minute of a task, ask 'What is not being covered?'. Take it up and tell the group.
suggestions.check: The group notices what you added.

suggestions.title: Ask 'who needs help'
suggestions.do: Check the group once or twice during the task and ask who needs a hand.
suggestions.how: Say it aloud: 'Does anyone need help?'. Then act on the answer.
suggestions.check: You are seen as an active part of the group.

suggestions.title: Join a team where your effort shows
suggestions.do: Play or serve in a team where your contribution is noticeable.
suggestions.how: A sport, a club project or a volunteer shift. Take a job that someone depends on.
suggestions.check: You bring effort without being pushed.

suggestions.title: Do the quiet job
suggestions.do: Take a task that nobody will notice, and do it well.
suggestions.how: Carry equipment, keep time, tidy up, note decisions. Do it without telling anyone.
suggestions.check: You feel fine when the credit goes to someone else.

suggestions.title: Give credit aloud
suggestions.do: Name someone else's contribution before you speak about your own.
suggestions.how: Say 'Ravi's point on time helped us...'. Do this at least twice per session.
suggestions.check: The group sees you as generous and your credit follows naturally.

suggestions.title: Ask 'what does the group need'
suggestions.do: Before you act, ask what the group needs most, not what looks best.
suggestions.how: Pause for five seconds before taking on a role. Pick what the group needs.
suggestions.check: Your role matches the task, not the audience.

suggestions.title: Support a rival's idea
suggestions.do: Back an idea from someone you compete with.
suggestions.how: In GD or PGT practice, find merit in a rival's point and build on it.
suggestions.check: You gain trust and do not lose standing.

suggestions.title: Work with the person you like least
suggestions.do: Pick the person you click with least and team up with them on a task.
suggestions.how: Give the task full effort. Notice what they are good at and say so.
suggestions.check: You work with them with no tension.

suggestions.title: Same help for everyone
suggestions.do: Offer the same help to everyone in the group.
suggestions.how: Keep a mental count of whom you helped. If someone is missing, help them next.
suggestions.check: Everyone gets your help equally.

suggestions.title: Task first, people second
suggestions.do: When you disagree with someone, go back to the task.
suggestions.how: Ask 'What helps the task here?' before you react to the person.
suggestions.check: Personal feelings stop deciding who you work with.

suggestions.title: Mixed team practice
suggestions.do: Practise tasks in groups assigned by others and not chosen by you.
suggestions.how: Ask a mentor to assign groups. Complete the task with whoever you get.
suggestions.check: You adapt to any team.

suggestions.title: Ask three people before you decide
suggestions.do: Collect three views before you commit to a plan.
suggestions.how: Ask each person one question and note their point. Include at least one in the final plan.
suggestions.check: Others see the plan as shared.

suggestions.title: Let go of your plan in one round
suggestions.do: Deliberately follow someone else's plan in a practice round.
suggestions.how: Support their idea fully and do not undermine it. Review what worked afterwards.
suggestions.check: You see value in plans that are not yours.

suggestions.title: Ask 'what do you think' and wait
suggestions.do: After you state your plan, ask for objections and wait a full ten seconds.
suggestions.how: Do not defend at once. Write the objection down and respond after.
suggestions.check: Others feel safe to disagree and the plan improves.

suggestions.title: Argue the group's side
suggestions.do: Defend a view that is not yours and see what the group sees.
suggestions.how: Take the group's view and give its best case.
suggestions.check: You hold views loosely and agree when the group is right.

suggestions.title: Finish your part, then ask who else needs help
suggestions.do: As soon as your part is done, check on others.
suggestions.how: Say 'My part is done, who needs help?'. Then act.
suggestions.check: You are seen as someone who helps, not only completes.

suggestions.title: Watch the whole task
suggestions.do: Track the group's progress, not only your part.
suggestions.how: Every minute, glance at the whole task and ask 'where are we stuck?'.
suggestions.check: You step in before the group is in trouble.

suggestions.title: Take a shared job
suggestions.do: Take on a role that depends on others.
suggestions.how: Be the timekeeper, the scribe or the coordinator in a group practice.
suggestions.check: You connect people and do not work alone.

suggestions.title: Help someone outside your tasks
suggestions.do: Do something for the group that nobody has assigned.
suggestions.how: One unasked act per session. A drink of water, a note, a clean-up.
suggestions.check: Your help is seen as part of your nature.

suggestions.title: Act before being asked
suggestions.do: Step in to fill a gap within the first minute.
suggestions.how: Scan the situation for the most important unmet need and handle it.
suggestions.check: Others describe you as someone who just gets on with it.

suggestions.title: Bring the quiet member in
suggestions.do: Make sure every member contributes to the task.
suggestions.how: Invite the quietest member by name to give their view.
suggestions.check: Group output improves.

olq.name: Sense of Responsibility
olq.meaning: How far you own a task or a duty, see it through, and accept the outcome, including the part that goes wrong.
olq.trainNote: SOR is a core quality. It grows through small, tracked commitments and honest review of failures. A tick of 8 is a not-recommended factor.

tick.6: Adequate. You take duties seriously and see them through. The step up is owning the outcome beyond your own task.
tick.7: Restricted. You are responsible for what is assigned to you, but not much beyond it, and sometimes slip under pressure.
tick.8: Limitation. Responsibility is selective, self-focused, deflected or inconsistent.
tick.9: Serious limitation. Duties are avoided or dropped, so the basics of ownership need rebuilding.

olq.strength: Strength. You own duties fully and see them through. Keep taking on larger and shared duties.

patterns.label: Responsible only for own assigned task

seen.6: Takes duties seriously and mainly the assigned ones.
seen.7: Does the assigned part well and does not look beyond it.
seen.8: Narrow view of duty. Own part is done and the group outcome is nobody's concern.
seen.9: Does not accept even assigned duties fully.

patterns.root: Sees duty as a list of tasks and not as an outcome to own.

patterns.label: Responsible for own interest first

seen.6: Responsible, with some attention to own performance.
seen.7: Takes on duties that help their own standing.
seen.8: Self-oriented. Takes the visible duty and avoids the one that costs them.
seen.9: Duty is a means to personal gain only.

patterns.root: Self-image and gain steer which duties are accepted.

patterns.label: Deflects blame, explains failure away

seen.6: Owns most mistakes and sometimes explains them away.
seen.7: Admits mistakes with explanations and external reasons.
seen.8: Blames others, circumstances or luck for failures.
seen.9: Denies responsibility and refuses to own errors.

patterns.root: Fear of being judged. Failure is felt as a threat to self-worth.

patterns.label: Waits to be told

seen.6: Reliable, and sometimes waits for a push.
seen.7: Carries out duty when told and does not self-start.
seen.8: Waits for orders. Does not take ownership of anything without being told.
seen.9: Avoids duty unless forced.

patterns.root: Low confidence or low drive. Prefers not to be wrong.

patterns.label: Starts well, drops off

seen.6: Reliable, with occasional lapses under pressure.
seen.7: Starts well and follow-through weakens when it gets hard or boring.
seen.8: Inconsistent. Commitments slip and need reminders.
seen.9: Unreliable. Duties are often left incomplete.

patterns.root: Enthusiasm without systems. No tracking of commitments.

patterns.label: Consolidate and stretch

seen.5: Strength. Keep taking on larger and shared duties.
seen.6: Responsible and reliable. Gains come from owning the whole outcome.

patterns.root: Strong base. The gap to a stronger tick is ownership beyond own task.

suggestions.title: Own the outcome, not the task
suggestions.do: In each group task, ask 'Did the group reach its aim?' at the end, not only 'Did I finish my part?'
suggestions.how: Before the task ends, check the whole result and fix any gaps you can reach.
suggestions.check: You speak of the group's result as yours.

suggestions.title: Take one extra duty a week
suggestions.do: Pick one duty outside your usual role and own it from start to end.
suggestions.how: Plan an event, hold the keys, run a small drive. Tell someone it is yours.
suggestions.check: The duty is done without reminders.

suggestions.title: Check on the whole group's work
suggestions.do: Check the team's progress at least twice during every task.
suggestions.how: Ask 'Where are we on this?' and help where the gap is.
suggestions.check: You catch problems before they grow.

suggestions.title: Be the last to leave the job
suggestions.do: Stay until the whole group's task is wrapped up.
suggestions.how: Tidy, check, note what remains. Do not leave when your own part ends.
suggestions.check: You leave only when everything is closed out.

suggestions.title: Take the duty nobody wants
suggestions.do: Volunteer for the least attractive job in the group.
suggestions.how: Cleaning, carrying, recording. Do it without telling anyone.
suggestions.check: The group sees you as someone who does what is needed.

suggestions.title: Put the group's result first
suggestions.do: In each task, name the group's aim before your own role.
suggestions.how: Open every plan with 'The aim is...'. Pick the role that serves it.
suggestions.check: Your role fits the task and not the audience.

suggestions.title: Accept a duty that costs you
suggestions.do: Take a task that costs you time or comfort, with nothing in return.
suggestions.how: Help a classmate prepare, run a session for juniors, cover a shift.
suggestions.check: You feel fine without reward.

suggestions.title: Quiet service log
suggestions.do: Keep a short log of duties you did that no one saw.
suggestions.how: One line each evening. Review weekly and aim to grow the list.
suggestions.check: Service becomes a habit and you stop tracking who noticed.

suggestions.title: Say 'my mistake' once a day
suggestions.do: Name your own error aloud, plainly, once a day.
suggestions.how: Pick the real error. Say 'I did X wrong, and next time I will do Y'. No excuse.
suggestions.check: Admitting a mistake feels ordinary and not threatening.

suggestions.title: Keep a failure log without excuses
suggestions.do: Write each failure with your own part in it and no external causes.
suggestions.how: Three lines: what happened, what I did, what I will change. Review weekly.
suggestions.check: Your log shows a pattern you can fix.

suggestions.title: Separate explanation from excuse
suggestions.do: Give the reason for a failure only after you own it.
suggestions.how: Say 'I own this' first and then give the context if it helps.
suggestions.check: People trust you more because you own errors first.

suggestions.title: Take the blame in a safe setting
suggestions.do: Volunteer to take responsibility for a small group failure.
suggestions.how: When a practice round fails, say 'That was on me' and say what you would change.
suggestions.check: Owning failure no longer feels like a loss.

suggestions.title: Start without being told
suggestions.do: Begin a useful action before anyone instructs you.
suggestions.how: In each task, identify the first action and say 'I will start with this'.
suggestions.check: You are seen as someone who starts.

suggestions.title: Take a duty of your own at home
suggestions.do: Hold a permanent household duty and do it without reminders.
suggestions.how: Pick a daily job like groceries, bills or cooking. Do it for 8 weeks without a single reminder.
suggestions.check: The duty runs without prompts.

suggestions.title: Make small decisions yourself
suggestions.do: Make and own five small decisions a day without asking.
suggestions.how: Choices of route, order, plan. Note what happens and learn.
suggestions.check: You decide quickly and own the result.

suggestions.title: Lead a small activity
suggestions.do: Take charge of one small activity from start to end.
suggestions.how: A study group, a sports session, a family trip. Own every part.
suggestions.check: You carry a duty from start to finish.

suggestions.title: Write commitments and tick them
suggestions.do: Write every commitment on a list and tick it off when done.
suggestions.how: Keep a daily list of five commitments. At night count how many were finished.
suggestions.check: You finish more than 80 percent of your commitments.

suggestions.title: Finish one boring task a day
suggestions.do: Complete one task you dislike every day.
suggestions.how: Start it first and finish before anything else. Do not move on until done.
suggestions.check: Finishing hard things becomes normal.

suggestions.title: Promise less, deliver all
suggestions.do: Make fewer commitments and keep all of them.
suggestions.how: Before saying yes, ask 'Can I really do this?'. If not, say no.
suggestions.check: People can rely on your word.

suggestions.title: Accountability partner
suggestions.do: Share your weekly commitments with a mentor or friend and report back.
suggestions.how: Send the list on Monday and report on Sunday. Count what was done.
suggestions.check: Follow-through becomes steady.

suggestions.title: Own the whole outcome of a group task
suggestions.do: Take on the full result of a group task, including the parts that belong to others.
suggestions.how: Check every part and step in where needed.
suggestions.check: The group's result is strong and you can explain every part.

suggestions.title: Take a duty that has risk
suggestions.do: Take a duty where failure is possible and public.
suggestions.how: Own a plan, a decision or an event where the stakes are visible.
suggestions.check: You handle the stakes calmly and own the result.

olq.name: Initiative
olq.meaning: How readily you start something useful on your own, see what needs doing, and act without waiting to be pushed.
olq.trainNote: INI is trainable through habit. It improves quickly once the Aspirant understands why they wait, and builds a routine of small first moves.

tick.6: Adequate. You start useful action on your own. The step up is doing it earlier and with more originality.
tick.7: Restricted. You act when a need is obvious or after a nudge, and your ideas are routine.
tick.8: Limitation. You wait, act late, act aimlessly or act only for show.
tick.9: Serious limitation. You rarely act unless pushed, so the habit of starting needs building.

olq.strength: Strength. You start useful action early. Keep stretching to original and harder starts.

patterns.label: Waits for instructions or others to start

seen.6: Starts well, sometimes after a short wait.
seen.7: Acts when the need is obvious or after a lead from others.
seen.8: Passive. Waits for instructions or for others to start.
seen.9: Acts only when pushed.

patterns.root: Fear of being wrong, or waiting for certainty.

patterns.label: Acts, but only on routine ideas

seen.6: Starts useful action, usually of the expected kind.
seen.7: Takes initiative on familiar matters and rarely on new ones.
seen.8: Initiative is mundane and without originality.
seen.9: Cannot generate a self-started action.

patterns.root: Limited ideas to act on. Initiative follows the quality of thinking.

patterns.label: Acts late, after others have started

seen.6: Acts well, sometimes a beat behind others.
seen.7: Reacts rather than initiates, and starts after others.
seen.8: Late to act. Others take the lead and the moment passes.
seen.9: Acts after the moment has gone.

patterns.root: Over-thinking before moving. Wants the perfect plan first.

patterns.label: Initiative for show, not for the task

seen.6: Takes initiative, and some of it looks for attention.
seen.7: Starts things that are visible and avoids the quiet ones.
seen.8: Initiative is for display, to be seen leading.
seen.9: Starts for attention without regard for the task.

patterns.root: Wants to be noticed. The task is secondary.

patterns.label: Starts without thinking

seen.6: Acts quickly, sometimes before checking.
seen.7: Starts fast and corrects later.
seen.8: Acts without thought. Misdirected starts waste effort.
seen.9: Impulsive action that causes problems.

patterns.root: Mistakes motion for progress. Skips the pause to check the aim.

patterns.label: Consolidate and stretch

seen.5: Strength. Keep stretching to original and harder starts.
seen.6: Starts useful action on your own. Gains come from earlier, more original starts.

patterns.root: Strong base. The gap to a stronger tick is originality and earlier starts.

suggestions.title: First move in ten seconds
suggestions.do: In any task, make the first suggestion or action within ten seconds.
suggestions.how: Say 'Let me suggest we begin with...'. It does not need to be perfect. Adjust later.
suggestions.check: You start the group more often than not.

suggestions.title: Three starts a day
suggestions.do: Start three small useful things every day without being asked.
suggestions.how: Tidy a room, call a friend, fix a file. Keep a tick list.
suggestions.check: Starting becomes a habit and not an effort.

suggestions.title: Do first, ask after
suggestions.do: In safe situations, act first and report afterwards.
suggestions.how: Practise with small things at home or on a team. Say 'I did X because Y'.
suggestions.check: You are comfortable acting without permission.

suggestions.title: Allow yourself to be wrong
suggestions.do: Take one action each day that could turn out wrong.
suggestions.how: Make a call, offer an idea, start a talk. Note that nothing bad happens.
suggestions.check: Fear of error stops holding you back.

suggestions.title: Ask 'what else could I do'
suggestions.do: Before you act, find one less obvious way to act.
suggestions.how: List the obvious action, then add one unusual one. Choose the better.
suggestions.check: Your starts include fresh ideas.

suggestions.title: Notice what is missing
suggestions.do: Spend a minute in any place noting what is missing or broken.
suggestions.how: Do it in a room, a campus, a market. Pick one item and fix or improve it.
suggestions.check: You see gaps easily and act on them.

suggestions.title: Improve one thing a week
suggestions.do: Pick one process at home or college and improve it.
suggestions.how: A queue, a schedule, a storage. Make a change and watch the effect.
suggestions.check: You can show a change that worked.

suggestions.title: Build your base of ideas
suggestions.do: Read, observe and collect solutions from different fields.
suggestions.how: Keep a notebook of ideas you saw. Add two per week and use one.
suggestions.check: You draw on a wider set of ideas when you act.

suggestions.title: Use a timer to start
suggestions.do: Set a 60 second timer and begin before it ends.
suggestions.how: Pick any task. Start the timer and begin action. Refine afterwards.
suggestions.check: You start before the pause becomes a habit.

suggestions.title: Good enough first
suggestions.do: Begin with a rough version and improve.
suggestions.how: Make a rough plan in 30 seconds, then start. Fix as you go.
suggestions.check: You no longer wait for the perfect plan.

suggestions.title: Be the first speaker in GD practice
suggestions.do: Aim to open the discussion in every practice GD.
suggestions.how: Prepare an opening line for common topics. Use it first.
suggestions.check: You lead the opening and the discussion follows.

suggestions.title: Shrink the decision
suggestions.do: Cut decisions to two options and choose in under a minute.
suggestions.how: Use a timer. Pick and move. Review the quality after.
suggestions.check: You decide fast without regret.

suggestions.title: Pick the task, not the spotlight
suggestions.do: Take initiative on something where the group benefits and nobody sees.
suggestions.how: Prepare, organise or fix something before the group arrives.
suggestions.check: You are comfortable with unseen initiative.

suggestions.title: Ask what the task needs
suggestions.do: Before you step up, ask what the task needs most.
suggestions.how: Take the role that helps the group and not the one that looks best.
suggestions.check: Your initiative is useful, not decorative.

suggestions.title: Step back, then step in
suggestions.do: Wait for a gap in the task and fill it quietly.
suggestions.how: Watch where the group is stuck. Fill that gap.
suggestions.check: The group accepts your initiative as help.

suggestions.title: Credit others for the result
suggestions.do: After a success, name others before yourself.
suggestions.how: Share credit in each debrief. Say what each person contributed.
suggestions.check: You feel secure without credit.

suggestions.title: Pause, aim, act
suggestions.do: Take a five second pause to state the aim before you start.
